sn.c: From row K back, the mezzanine overhang can cut off the top of the stage.
sn.sh: Mezzanine overhang can cut off the top of the stage

sn.c: Row A sits below stage level, close enough that some scenes are hard to take in comfortably.
sn.sh: Below stage level, so some scenes are hard to take in

sn.c: Toward the far sides of the Left and Right Orchestra the view turns side-on, and higher seat numbers are often sold as partial view.
sn.sh: Side-on view, often sold as partial view

sn.c: The far sides and back corners of the mezzanine have restricted views, and the rake gets steep in the last rows.
sn.sh: Restricted views, and steep in the last rows

sn.c: The middle rows of the Center Mezzanine are a price bracket below the front rows and keep a broad view of the stage.
sn.sh: Cheaper than the front rows, with a broad view of the stage

sn.c: In the Left and Right Mezzanine, row G sits behind a cross aisle, so it has extra legroom and a clear look over the rows in front.
sn.sh: Behind a cross aisle, so there is extra legroom

sn.c: Mezzanine rows are tight on legroom, even for people of average height. Aisle seats have the most room.
sn.sh: Tight legroom, and aisle seats have the most room

vs.sum: The Al Hirschfeld Theatre offers generally good sightlines, though some seats have minor obstructions. The sound quality is above average, enhancing the theatrical experience. However, the seating is cramped, especially for taller patrons, which detracts from comfort. The theater's ambiance is rich with historical character, though restroom lines can be long during intermission.

acc.note: Orchestra-only wheelchair access. Infrared headsets and audio induction neck loops available.
